Medo-Persia
mē′dō-pΆŕ′zhă
n. (the combined Median-Persian empire of Daniel's prophecy, successor to Babylon)
A compound of Media and Persia, the two allied kingdoms whose combined empire, under Cyrus, overthrew Babylon and is named jointly throughout Daniel and Esther.

Biblical Definition

Medo-Persia is Scripture’s own compound reckoning of the empire that conquered Babylon and ruled the known world through the era of Daniel, Esther, Ezra, and Nehemiah — named jointly, and in that fixed order, again and again rather than treated as Persia alone. The handwriting on Belshazzar’s wall pronounces the verdict in these very terms: “PERES; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians” (Daniel 5:28), fulfilled that same night. Daniel’s vision of the ram with two horns is interpreted explicitly: “The ram which thou sawest having two horns are the kings of Media and Persia” (Daniel 8:20), the second, higher horn representing Persia’s eventual dominance within the alliance. The empire’s legal character — a fixed, unchangeable law, distinct from the personal despotism of Babylon — is twice made a matter of high drama: “the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” traps Daniel in the lions’ den (Daniel 6:8), and the same irrevocable “law of the Persians and the Medes” is invoked to seal Vashti’s deposing in Esther 1:19. This dual empire is the silver kingdom of Nebuchadnezzar’s image (Daniel 2:39) and the bear of Daniel’s vision (Daniel 7:5), inferior to Babylon’s gold yet the LORD’s own appointed instrument to end the captivity and send Cyrus to rebuild the temple (Ezra 1:1–2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry under this compound form; Medo-Persia is the joint Median-Persian empire of Daniel's prophecies, whose fixed, unalterable law and eventual overthrow of Babylon are recorded across Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther.

expand to see more

MEDO-PERSIA, n. The combined empire of the Medes and Persians, successor to Babylon, prominent in the prophecies of Daniel.

PERSIA, n. An ancient empire of southwestern Asia, whose kings, beginning with Cyrus, permitted the Jews' return from captivity.

MEDE, n. A native or inhabitant of Media, an ancient country allied with, and eventually absorbed into, the Persian empire.

IRREVOCABLE, a. Incapable of being recalled, revoked, or annulled; unalterable.

PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over His creatures, directing even the decrees of pagan empires.

Key Scripture

Daniel 5:28 — "PERES; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians."

Daniel 8:20 — "The ram which thou sawest having two horns are the kings of Media and Persia."

Daniel 6:8 — "Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not."

Esther 1:19 — "If it please the king, let there go a royal commandment from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, that it be not altered, That Vashti come no more before king Ahasuerus; and let the king give her royal estate unto another that is better than she."

Modern Corruption

Prophecy naming, in advance, a specific two-part empire with a legal character unlike its predecessor's and its consequent overthrow of Babylon is a poor fit for a book critics insist was written after the fact.

expand to see more

Critical scholarship that dates the book of Daniel to the second century BC, precisely to explain away its apparent foreknowledge of Medo-Persia's rise and fall, still cannot account for the accuracy of secondary details embedded incidentally in the narrative — the peculiar, historically attested fact of an unalterable royal law unique to this empire (Daniel 6:8; Esther 1:19) is exactly the kind of texture a writer working centuries after the fact, from garbled memory, would be unlikely to preserve so precisely.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Daniel's own doxology upon receiving these very visions: “he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Daniel 2:21). Medo-Persia's rise to overthrow Babylon and its own later fall to Greece were not accidents of history but the LORD's own ordering of Gentile empires toward the fixed goal of Christ's kingdom, which alone “shall never be destroyed” (Daniel 2:44).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew/Aramaic Maday (H4074), Media; Paras (H6539), Persia; malkuth (H4437), kingdom; shena' (H8133), to change, alter.

expand to see more

Aramaic Maday (H4074) — Media; the first element of the compound name.

Aramaic Paras (H6539) — Persia; the second, and eventually dominant, element.

Aramaic malkuth (H4437) — kingdom; the word of Daniel 5:28's pronouncement.

Aramaic shena' (H8133) — to change, alter; the very thing the Medo-Persian law could not do.

Hebrew dath (H1881) — law, decree; the fixed legal character of the empire in Esther and Daniel.

Usage

"“Given to the Medes and Persians” — the verdict of the handwriting on the wall."

"“The kings of Media and Persia” — Gabriel's interpretation of the two-horned ram."

"“The law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” — the empire's fixed legal character."
